title: Core communication skills
blurb: Listen actively, read cues, choose open or closed questions well and check understanding every time.
question: A patient says 'I'm fine' about tomorrow's surgery while gripping the bed rail and avoiding eye contact. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse?

teach.h: Communication is listening as much as talking
teach.body: Annexe A of the NMC proficiency standards lists the core skills: actively listening and responding to verbal and non-verbal cues, using prompts and positive reinforcement, appropriate touch, eye contact and personal space, open and closed questions, caring conversations, and checking understanding. Code 7 adds using terms people understand, a range of verbal and non-verbal methods with cultural sensitivity, and checking understanding from time to time.

values: Trust the non-verbal cue, explore it

teach.caption: When words and body language do not match, the body language often tells you more.

teach.caption: Start open to explore, then use closed questions to confirm specific details.

teach.body: Active listening means giving full attention, showing you are listening and reflecting back what you hear. Use minimal prompts ('go on', a nod), paraphrase ('so you are worried about…'), reflect feelings ('you sound frightened') and summarise. Allow silence: it gives people time to think. Positive reinforcement ('you have done really well with your exercises') encourages people to keep going.

steps.label: Prepare
steps.sub: privacy, time, sit at their level

teach.h: Worked scenario: Nurse Hana on a surgical ward
teach.body: Mr Novak, 58, says he is 'fine' about his bowel surgery, but grips the bed rail and will not look at her. Hana sits down at his eye level, closes the curtain and says, 'You said you're fine, but you look tense. How are you really feeling about tomorrow?' She waits through a long pause. He admits he fears waking with a stoma. Hana reflects this back, answers his questions and arranges for the stoma nurse to visit.

teach.h: Touch, eye contact and personal space
items: Ask or explain before touching; use touch to comfort only when welcome.
Eye contact shows attention, but norms differ between cultures and people: follow the person's lead (Code 7.3).
Respect personal space; sit rather than stand over someone in bed.
Some people, including some autistic people, may find eye contact or touch uncomfortable: adapt.

teach.caption: NICE NG197 (2021) recommends chunk and check and teach-back to check understanding.

teach.text: 'Do you understand?' is a CLOSED question that most people answer 'yes'. To check understanding, use teach-back: 'Can you tell me in your own words how you will take these tablets?'

items: Listen actively: attend, prompt, paraphrase, reflect, summarise and allow silence.
Notice non-verbal cues, especially when they clash with what people say.
Open questions explore; closed questions confirm; avoid leading questions.
Check understanding with teach-back and chunk and check (Code 7.4; NG197).

summary: You can now listen actively, respond to verbal and non-verbal cues and choose open or closed questions to suit the purpose. You can also use touch, eye contact and space sensitively and check understanding with teach-back.

options: 'What worries you most about going home?'
'Are you worried about going home?'
'You're happy to go home today, aren't you?'
'Is your daughter collecting you at noon?'
A.why: Open questions invite a full answer in the person's own words and cannot be answered with yes or no.

whyNot.1: This can be answered yes or no, so it is closed.
whyNot.2: This is a leading question that suggests the expected answer.
whyNot.3: This is a closed question seeking a specific fact.

A.q: A nurse wants to check that a patient understands how to use her new inhaler. Which approach is best?
options: Ask 'Do you understand how to use it?'
Give her a leaflet to read later
Repeat the explanation more slowly
Ask her to show how she will use it
A.why: Teach-back, where the person explains or demonstrates in their own way, checks understanding (Code 7.4; Annexe A 1.6; NICE NG197).

whyNot.0: A yes or no answer does not show what she actually understands.
whyNot.1: A leaflet can support learning but does not check understanding now.
whyNot.2: Repetition may help, but it does not check what she has understood.

A.q: A nurse says 'Go on…' and nods while a patient describes his symptoms. What technique is this?
options: Summarising
Using a minimal prompt
Closed questioning
Reflecting feelings
A.why: Minimal prompts such as nods and 'go on' encourage the person to keep talking (Annexe A 1.2).

whyNot.0: Summarising draws together the main points at the end.
whyNot.2: A closed question asks for a specific fact.
whyNot.3: Reflecting feelings names the emotion the person seems to be expressing.

B.q: A patient says she is 'not bothered' about her biopsy results but keeps twisting her hands and looking at the door. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept her answer and move on to observations
Reassure her that most results are normal
Gently name what she has noticed and invite her to talk
Ask the doctor to prescribe something for anxiety
B.why: Responding to non-verbal cues that clash with what is said is part of active listening (Annexe A 1.1; Code 2.6).

whyNot.0: This misses clear non-verbal signs of distress.
whyNot.1: False reassurance closes the conversation and may be wrong.
whyNot.3: Exploring her worries comes before considering medication.

B.q: A nurse says to a patient, 'It sounds as though you feel let down by the delay.' What technique is she using?
options: Closed questioning
Reflecting feelings
Giving advice
Changing the subject
B.why: Reflecting feelings names the emotion behind what the person has said, showing empathy and checking accuracy.

whyNot.0: No question requiring yes or no is asked.
whyNot.3: The nurse stays with the patient's topic.

B.q: During an admission assessment, the nurse needs to know whether a patient has any allergies. Which question is most appropriate?
options: 'Tell me about your health over the years.'
'How do you feel about being in hospital?'
'You haven't got any allergies, have you?'
'Do you have any allergies to medicines or foods?'
B.why: A closed question is best for confirming a specific fact such as allergies, after open questions have explored wider concerns.

whyNot.0: This open question explores history but may not elicit allergy information.
whyNot.2: This is a leading question that invites 'no'.

C.q: An older woman from a culture where direct eye contact with professionals is considered disrespectful looks down while the nurse talks. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Adapt to her preference and check understanding verbally
Ask her to look up so the nurse can assess her mood
Record that she is avoiding engagement
Ask her relative to explain instead
C.why: Code 7.3: use a range of communication methods and consider cultural sensitivities. Adapt and check understanding in other ways.

whyNot.1: Insisting on eye contact ignores her cultural norms.
whyNot.2: Recording avoidance is an incorrect assumption about her behaviour.
whyNot.3: Bypassing her removes her from her own care.

C.q: A nurse explains a new insulin regimen in one long explanation. The patient nods throughout but later gives the wrong dose. What would have best prevented this?
options: A longer single explanation
Using more medical terms for accuracy
Chunk and check with teach-back
Asking 'Is that clear?' at the end
C.why: NICE NG197 recommends delivering information in manageable chunks and checking understanding, for example with teach-back, before moving on.

whyNot.0: More information at once makes overload worse.
whyNot.1: Code 7.1 asks for terms people understand, not more jargon.
whyNot.3: 'Is that clear?' is closed and usually gets 'yes'.

C.q: A distressed man is sitting in silence after being told his wife is very unwell. The nurse is sitting with him. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Fill the silence with reassurance
Step away to give him some privacy
Change the subject to practical matters
Stay with him and allow the silence
C.why: Allowing silence gives the person time to process and shows the nurse is present and listening (Annexe A 1.1, 1.5).

whyNot.0: Rushing to fill silence can feel dismissive and offer false reassurance.
whyNot.1: Leaving may feel like abandonment; staying shows care. He can say if he wants to be alone.
whyNot.2: Moving to practicalities too quickly does not respond to his distress.

reteach.title: Funnel your questions
reteach.question: How do you get both the whole story and the exact detail?

blocks.body: Start with a wide, open question so the person can tell you what matters to them. Use prompts and reflection to keep them talking. Then narrow down with closed questions to pin down specific facts, such as when the pain started. Finish by summarising and checking you have understood each other.

blocks.text: Leading questions ('You're not in pain, are you?') push people towards the answer you expect. Avoid them.

explain.body: Attend fully, use prompts, paraphrase, reflect feelings, summarise and allow silence.

test.q: At the end of a conversation a nurse says, 'So, the main things worrying you are the pain at night and how you'll manage the stairs.' What is this?
options: A leading question
Summarising
Positive reinforcement
A closed question
test.why: Summarising draws together the main points to check shared understanding (Annexe A 1.6).

whyNot.2: Positive reinforcement praises effort or progress.
whyNot.3: It is a statement, not a yes or no question.

explain.body: Open questions explore; closed questions confirm facts; leading questions push an answer and should be avoided.

options: 'Have you opened your bowels today?'
'How are you finding the new diet?'
'What would help you sleep better?'
'Tell me about your pain.'
test.why: A closed question can be answered yes or no, or with a single fact.

whyNot.1: This invites a description, so it is open.
whyNot.2: This invites the person's own ideas, so it is open.
whyNot.3: This invites a full account, so it is open.

explain.body: Use touch, eye contact and personal space appropriately, adapting to culture and individual preference.

test.q: A nurse is about to discuss a care plan with a patient in bed. Where should she position herself?
options: Standing at the end of the bed
Standing over the bed to be heard
Sitting at the patient's eye level
Behind the patient, out of sight
test.why: Sitting at eye level respects personal space, reduces the power imbalance and supports eye contact (Annexe A 1.3).

whyNot.0: Standing at a distance feels formal and rushed.
whyNot.1: Standing over the patient is intimidating.
whyNot.3: Being out of sight prevents non-verbal communication.

explain.body: Check understanding from time to time (Code 7.4). Use teach-back and chunk and check rather than 'Do you understand?'.

test.q: Which Code standard asks nurses to check people's understanding from time to time to keep misunderstanding or mistakes to a minimum?
test.why: Code 7.4: check people's understanding from time to time to keep misunderstanding or mistakes to a minimum.

whyNot.1: 7.2 is meeting language and communication needs.
